**Prerequisites**
To run all the code in this manuscript, you will need the following software:
- FreeSurfer
- SimNIBS
- python
- git
- yq
We recommend you build a virtual environment for the python framework using conda. It is important that you use python version 3.11, the newest python version that lets all the used dependencies coexist. The virtual environment should then contain the mindmap package, specifically designed to hold any functions related to this project.
```bash
cd ~/location/for/mindmap/package
git clone https://github.com/NinoHerve/mindmap.git

cd ~/location/for/manuscript/project
git clone https://github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET.git

conda create -n <env-name> python=3.11
conda activate <env-name>
pip install .
```
You should now be ready to run anything that comes ahead.

# Materials and Methods

## Source Reconstruction Pipeline

### Source Space — Additional Implementation Details

**Surface reconstruction and dipole placement.** The cortical surface was reconstructed using FreeSurfer (v7.4.1). Dipoles were placed via an oct6 icosahedral subdivision (after excluding medial-wall and non-cortical vertices) using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013).

**Orientation-constraint rationale.** Dipole orientations were fixed normal to the cortical manifold — a constraint widely adopted in distributed source reconstruction because the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, pyramidal neurons, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the cortical surface [@dale_improved_1993]. For the connectivity-informed methods, the constraint is also a structural requirement. The connectome describes connections between pairs of fixed cortical locations. Each location carries a single scalar source amplitude. A free-orientation dipole instead has three orthogonal components, which have no counterpart in the connectome.

### Volume Conduction Model — Additional Implementation Details

**Head-model pipeline.** Brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template, each surface constrained in turn to stay outside its inner neighbor's already-fitted surface (skin fitted last, constrained by the outer skull; outer skull constrained by the inner skull) — the "sequential and non-intersecting" fitting referenced in the main text.

**Skull-base limitation.** The boundary element method requires each tissue compartment to be a closed, watertight surface, but the true skull base is not: openings such as the foramen magnum and the smaller foramina nerves and vessels pass through break that assumption. Rather than attempt to model this genuinely perforated geometry, our fitting procedure simply closes the skull surfaces off smoothly below a fixed height, sacrificing anatomical accuracy at the very base of the skull by design. This is only acceptable if the resulting error stays away from the sources actually reconstructed here: @lanfer_skull_2012 found that errors from simplifying the inferior skull, while not negligible in general, concentrate in deep sources near the skull base (e.g., cerebellum) — a region this manuscript's cortical-surface-only source space never reconstructs from in the first place.

**Why the default watershed extraction is sub-optimal.** MNE-Python's default pipeline (`mne.bem.make_watershed_bem`, delegating to FreeSurfer's `mri_watershed`) fits the outer scalp surface directly from the T1 via a deformable surface fit, but T1-weighted MRI has poor bone contrast, so the inner and outer skull surfaces are not obtained the same principled way: the inner skull is instead approximated by expanding the brain mask outward by a fixed margin, and the outer skull by retracting the already-fit scalp surface inward, rather than by detecting the actual bone boundary. Neither is a genuine tissue-boundary detection step, which is why watershed-derived skull surfaces are a well-known source of geometry problems and MNE's own documentation recommends visually inspecting them before use — precisely the failure mode motivating this manuscript's custom CHARM-based pipeline instead.

**BEM comparison against MNE-Python's default watershed extraction.** To illustrate the sub-optimal geometries this produces, we additionally ran MNE-Python's default FreeSurfer watershed extraction (`mne.bem.make_watershed_bem`, FreeSurfer v7.4.1) on the flagship simulation subject (sub-10) and compared the resulting surfaces against the CHARM-based ones actually used for reconstruction (@tbl-bem-comparison). The default watershed geometry fails MNE's own BEM-construction check outright: calling `mne.make_bem_model` on it raises `RuntimeError: Surface inner skull is not completely inside surface outer skull`. Checking each compartment pair's nesting directly confirms why: 42/10,242 (0.41%) inner-skull vertices lie geometrically outside the outer-skull surface, and 4/10,242 (0.04%) outer-skull vertices lie outside the scalp, with the two skull surfaces coming within 0.32 mm of touching at their closest point. The CHARM-based pipeline's sequential, constrained fitting produces zero such violations by construction, with a comfortable 2.32 mm minimum gap between the skull surfaces, and its BEM model builds without error.

| Metric | MNE default watershed | Custom CHARM pipeline |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Inner-skull vertices outside outer-skull | 42 / 10,242 (0.41%) | 0 / 10,242 (0.00%) |
| Outer-skull vertices outside scalp | 4 / 10,242 (0.04%) | 0 / 10,242 (0.00%) |
| Minimum inner-to-outer-skull gap | 0.32 mm | 2.32 mm |
| Minimum outer-skull-to-scalp gap | 2.12 mm | 3.21 mm |
| `mne.make_bem_model` / `make_bem_solution` | Fails (nesting violation) | Succeeds |

: BEM geometry comparison for the simulation subject: MNE-Python's default watershed extraction vs. the custom CHARM-based pipeline used throughout this manuscript. {#tbl-bem-comparison}

**A second example where watershed does not fail outright.** The sub-10 case above is a hard failure — MNE refuses to build a BEM model at all. That is not the only failure mode: for subject sub-pat10 of the SPIKE resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A), the default watershed geometry *passes* MNE's nesting check (`mne.make_bem_model` and `mne.make_bem_solution` both succeed without error) and is still visibly wrong (@fig-bem-spike). Panel (a) shows CHARM's own tissue segmentation (`Bone-Cortical`/`Bone-Cancellous` in tan, `Skin` not shown) as anatomical reference for where the skull actually is — not independent ground truth, since panel (b)'s CHARM surface is fit directly from this same segmentation, but a meaningful check on panel (c)'s watershed surface, which never sees this segmentation at all. CHARM's outer-skull contour (panel b) closely follows the segmented bone boundary. Watershed's (panel c) does not: it balloons outward well past the true skull, consistent with the coarse expand-the-brain/retract-the-scalp heuristic described above rather than genuine bone detection.

**Skull-conductivity mismatch precedent.** A similar strategy — perturbing skull conductivity between the forward and inverse models to avoid the inverse crime — has been used elsewhere to probe the sensitivity of EEG source analysis to head-model mismatch [@vorwerk_skull_2014].

```{python filename="forward_mismatch_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import sys
import numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from scripts.data_manager import SimfManager

# Self-contained, like the other Annex sections above: reloads the two
# forward solutions actually used for Study I (Section 2.1.2) rather than
# hand-computing this offline - processing_simf.qmd does not itself compute
# this comparison, so there is no cached result to reuse here.
dm_fwd = SimfManager("../processing/simf.config.yml")
sub_fwd = "10"
fwd_sim = dm_fwd.load(sub_fwd, "fwd", desc="sim")
fwd_inv = dm_fwd.load(sub_fwd, "fwd", desc="inv")

G_sim = fwd_sim["sol"]["data"]
G_inv = fwd_inv["sol"]["data"]

# Relative difference measure (RDM): per-dipole leadfield columns normalized
# to unit norm (removing amplitude scaling), then the norm of their
# difference - a standard forward-model comparison metric quantifying
# topographic (shape) mismatch, of the kind used in the head-model-mismatch
# literature (@vorwerk_skull_2014). 0 = identical topography, 2 = inverted.
G_sim_n = G_sim / np.linalg.norm(G_sim, axis=0, keepdims=True)
G_inv_n = G_inv / np.linalg.norm(G_inv, axis=0, keepdims=True)
rdm = np.linalg.norm(G_sim_n - G_inv_n, axis=0)

fwd_n_dipoles = f"{G_sim.shape[1]:,}"
fwd_rdm_median = fmt_num(np.median(rdm) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_mean = fmt_num(np.mean(rdm) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_iqr_lo = fmt_num(np.percentile(rdm, 25) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_iqr_hi = fmt_num(np.percentile(rdm, 75) * 100, 1)
```

**Forward-model mismatch magnitude.** Comparing the two forward solutions' gain matrices directly for the flagship simulation subject (sub-10, `{python} fwd_n_dipoles`-dipole source space): the relative difference measure (RDM) — a standard forward-model comparison metric quantifying topographic (shape) differences independently of amplitude scaling, the relevant summary of forward-model *mismatch* since a source-reconstruction method invariant to overall amplitude scaling would not be biased by gain differences alone — has a median of `{python} fwd_rdm_median`% across dipoles (mean `{python} fwd_rdm_mean`%, IQR [`{python} fwd_rdm_iqr_lo`%, `{python} fwd_rdm_iqr_hi`%]), consistent with the "~10%" figure quoted in the main text.

### Connectivity Matrices — Additional Implementation Details

This section provides implementation-level detail for the connectivity matrices described in Section 2.1.3.

**Empirical connectomes.** Short-range links connect each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors on the cortical manifold, subject to two constraints: a maximum geodesic distance of 15 mm, and a maximum of 8 such neighbors per dipole. The 15 mm threshold is reasonably well-grounded: at this source space's resolution it excludes only ~1% of true (Euclidean) nearest-neighbor pairs from being connected — down from ~6.4% at an earlier, coarser source-space resolution — and it also falls within the ~5–30 mm range typically cited for U-fiber length scales. The 8-neighbor cap is a softer, less rigorously-grounded choice: raised from an earlier value of 3 simply to preserve similar relative local coverage after dipole density roughly tripled at the current resolution (candidate neighbors within 15 mm rose from ~35 to ~88 per dipole), rather than derived from an independent criterion of its own.

**Atlas surrogate.** The MultiConn atlas reference population used to define long-range tracts comprises 66 subjects, and a tract is retained only if present across all 66. Rather than connecting every dipole pair between two atlas-connected regions, only a fraction of the possible dipole-to-dipole edges is instantiated, at a sparsity level (14%) determined by matching the edge density of this same sub-10 subject's own empirical connectome (above) — the only subject in our sample with real tractography data available.

**Local surrogate.** Nodes are additionally connected across hemispheres to their homotopic (mirror-symmetric) partner to keep the resulting graph connected.

**Laplace-Beltrami surrogate (GBF).** Eigenmodes are computed using the `lapy` Python library (v1.6.0) for the underlying finite-element stiffness/mass matrix assembly. This mesh is the triangulation of the source space itself, in dipole space (Section 2.1.1) — the decimated, cortex-only surface used for the dipoles — rather than the dense FreeSurfer surface typically used for this computation. This matches @wang_geometry_2026's own approach: their Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes are likewise computed on their own downsampled, dipole-resolution source space (~10,000 dipoles per hemisphere for real data, ~4,000 per hemisphere for their benchmark simulations — comparable in spirit to this manuscript's own ~7,600-dipole source space) rather than the dense native FreeSurfer mesh; their Discussion's contrast against "coarse regional parcellations" refers to connectome/atlas-eigenmode approaches like CSET, not to mesh density.

**Harmonic localization (inverse participation ratio).** The Discussion hypothesizes that the true connectome underperforms its dMRI-free surrogates in Study I because its reconstruction-weighted harmonics are more spatially localized. @fig-ipr-harmonics quantifies this: for each condition, every harmonic's inverse participation ratio (IPR) — $\sum_i x_i^4$ for an orthonormal harmonic $x$, higher for harmonics concentrated on fewer dipoles — is weighted by wCSET's own reconstruction weight for that harmonic (Section 2.1.4) and averaged, excluding each condition's trivial constant mode(s) (maximally spread by construction, regardless of graph structure). The true connectome's weighted-mean IPR is higher than every graph-based surrogate's and higher than the Laplace-Beltrami surrogate's — consistent with a more rigid, spatially specific prior that helps only when it matches genuine tract-driven clustering.

```{python filename="simf_ipr_harmonics_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-ipr-harmonics
#| fig-cap: "Reconstruction-weighted mean inverse participation ratio (IPR) of each condition's harmonics — the basis wCSET's spatial prior is built from. Higher IPR means harmonics concentrated on fewer, sometimes spatially disjoint dipoles; lower IPR means harmonics that vary smoothly across the cortex. The true connectome (original) produces more localized harmonics than every dMRI-free surrogate."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from scripts.data_manager import SimfManager

# Reproduces surrogate_harmonics_investigation.ipynb's weighted-mean-IPR
# result under the reader-facing surrogate names used throughout this
# manuscript (Section 2.1.3) rather than the on-disk `Surrogate` tags.
dm_ipr = SimfManager("../processing/simf.config.yml")
sub_ipr = "10"

LOWPASS_CONDS = ["original", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
HARM = 5
LOGPASS_CUTOFF = 150
ALL_CONDS = LOWPASS_CONDS + ["beltrami"]

IPR_LABELS = {
    "original": "original", "beltrami": "Beltrami (GBF)",
    "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}
IPR_COLORS = {
    "original": LINE_COLOR, "beltrami": "#2a78d6",
    "fused": "#eb6834", "fused-bin": "#1baf7a",
    "geom-atlas": "#eda100", "geom-atlas-bin": "#e87ba4",
}

def _load_eig(desc):
    kwargs = {} if desc == "original" else {"desc": desc}
    eig = dm_ipr.load(sub_ipr, "eig", **kwargs)
    return eig["vec"], eig["val"]

eigs_ipr = {d: _load_eig(d) for d in ALL_CONDS}

# wCSET's own reconstruction weight per harmonic (Section 2.1.4): exponential
# lowpass (harm=5) for the true connectome and its four graph-based
# surrogates, GBF's logpass/cutoff=150 for beltrami - the same two
# weighting mechanisms used throughout the manuscript, not recomputed
# differently here.
def _lowpass_weight(val, harm=HARM):
    return np.exp(-harm * val)

def _logpass_weight(val, cutoff=LOGPASS_CUTOFF):
    w = np.zeros_like(val)
    lam_cutoff = val[cutoff - 1]
    normalized = np.clip(val[:cutoff] / lam_cutoff, 1e-8, 1.0)
    w[:cutoff] = np.sqrt(-np.log(normalized))
    return w

weights_ipr = {name: _lowpass_weight(eigs_ipr[name][1]) for name in LOWPASS_CONDS}
weights_ipr["beltrami"] = _logpass_weight(eigs_ipr["beltrami"][1])

# Inverse participation ratio: IPR = sum(x_i^4) for an orthonormal harmonic x
# (sum(x_i^2)=1) - a condensed-matter-physics measure of how localized a
# wavefunction (here, a cortical harmonic) is.
def _ipr(eigvec):
    p = eigvec ** 2
    return np.sum(p ** 2, axis=0)

iprs_ipr = {name: _ipr(eigs_ipr[name][0]) for name in ALL_CONDS}

# Reconstruction-weighted mean IPR, one number per condition - excludes each
# condition's trivial constant/near-constant mode(s) (k=0 for the graph
# Laplacian conditions; k=0,1 for beltrami, one per independently-solved
# hemisphere), which carry the top weight by construction but are, by
# definition, maximally spread out regardless of graph structure.
ipr_summary = {}
for name in LOWPASS_CONDS:
    w, p = weights_ipr[name][1:], iprs_ipr[name][1:]
    ipr_summary[name] = np.sum(w * p) / np.sum(w)
w_b, p_b = weights_ipr["beltrami"][2:], iprs_ipr["beltrami"][2:]
ipr_summary["beltrami"] = np.sum(w_b * p_b) / np.sum(w_b)

ipr_order = ["original", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin", "beltrami"]

ipr_fig, ipr_ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
ipr_ax.bar(
    range(len(ipr_order)), [ipr_summary[n] for n in ipr_order],
    color=[IPR_COLORS[n] for n in ipr_order],
)
ipr_ax.set_ylabel("Reconstruction-weighted mean IPR")
ipr_ax.set_xticks(range(len(ipr_order)))
ipr_ax.set_xticklabels([IPR_LABELS[n] for n in ipr_order], rotation=30, ha="right")
ipr_ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
```

```{python filename="simf_ipr_example_stats.py"}
#| output: false
# Harmonic 139: concentrated on a few patches in the empirical connectome, spread across the cortex in
# the binarized atlas surrogate (same harmonic index, so a similar position in the spectrum). Values
# quoted in the prose; the figure itself is a prepared image (results/simf/ipr_example_harmonic139.png).
ipr_ex_k = 139
ipr_ex_conds = {"original": "empirical", "fused-bin": "binarized atlas"}
ipr_ex = {c: (float(eigs_ipr[c][1][ipr_ex_k]), float(iprs_ipr[c][ipr_ex_k])) for c in ipr_ex_conds}
ipr_ex_lam_orig, ipr_ex_lam_atlas = (fmt_num(ipr_ex[c][0], 3) for c in ipr_ex_conds)
ipr_ex_ipr_orig, ipr_ex_ipr_atlas = (f"{ipr_ex[c][1]:.3g}" for c in ipr_ex_conds)

```

To make "IPR" concrete, @fig-ipr-example shows the same harmonic (k = `{python} ipr_ex_k`) for the empirical connectome and for the binarized atlas surrogate. In the empirical connectome, the harmonic concentrates on a few patches of one hemisphere (circled; IPR = `{python} ipr_ex_ipr_orig`, λ = `{python} ipr_ex_lam_orig`). In the atlas surrogate, it spreads across both hemispheres (IPR = `{python} ipr_ex_ipr_atlas`, about `{python} ipr_ex_ratio` times lower; λ = `{python} ipr_ex_lam_atlas`). This is what "more spatially concentrated" means for the empirical connectome's weighted-mean IPR above: not that every harmonic it relies on looks like the left panel, but that its harmonics tend further in that direction than the surrogates'.

The empirical harmonic concentrates on a few patches of one hemisphere (circled); the atlas harmonic spreads across both hemispheres. λ₁₃₉: graph frequency (eigenvalue) of the harmonic; IPR: inverse participation ratio (higher = more spatially concentrated).](../results/simf/ipr_example_harmonic139.png){#fig-ipr-example}


### Inverse Problem and Methods — Additional Details

**Standard inverse solutions — full derivation.** This section provides the full derivation of the standard inverse solutions (wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA) introduced in Section 2.1.4.

From a Bayesian perspective, $\mathbf s$ is treated as a random variable with a prior distribution $P(\mathbf s)$ [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Assuming a Gaussian prior $\mathbf s \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma_{\mathbf s})$, reconstruction becomes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, leading to the optimization problem given in Eq. (1) of the main text. There, $\mathbf C$ acts as a weighting matrix derived from the prior covariance, such that $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$. In practice, the true source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ is unknown. sLORETA and dSPM replace it with the identity matrix, i.e. independent sources with equal variance. wMNE replaces it with a diagonal depth-weighting matrix (below): its sources are still independent a priori, but deep sources receive larger variances. This diagonal prior, shared by all three methods, is why we call them connectivity-agnostic throughout this work.

For wMNE, the depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ counteracts the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles:

$$
\mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s} = \mathbf W_d^2, \qquad \text{where} \quad W_{d,ii} = \lVert \mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}
$$

so that deep sources, with small lead-field norms, receive a larger prior variance. In the SVD form of the main text, $\mathbf B=\mathbf W_d$.

For wMNE, the depth-weighting exponent was set to $\kappa=2$, within the 2.0–5.0 range that @lin_assessing_2006 found optimal for EEG (MNE-Python's default, 0.8, is the value for MEG). In simulation, κ = 2 gave slightly larger localization errors than κ = 0.8, and wMNE remained the least accurate method with either value. sLORETA and dSPM apply an additional post-hoc standardization on top of the minimum-norm estimate, and were run without additional depth weighting, since this noise-normalization step already compensates for depth bias on its own.

With $\mathbf B=\mathbf I$ and the SVD $\mathbf L=\mathbf E_f\boldsymbol\Gamma\mathbf E_\ell^\top$ of the main text, both standardizations divide the minimum-norm estimate $s^*_k$ of source $k$ by a norm computed from the same decomposition:

$$
z_k^{\text{dSPM}}=\frac{s^*_k}{\lVert[\mathbf E_\ell\mathbf D_\lambda]_{k,:}\rVert},\qquad
z_k^{\text{sLORETA}}=\frac{s^*_k}{\big\lVert[\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathrm{diag}(\gamma_j/\sqrt{\gamma_j^2+\lambda})]_{k,:}\big\rVert}
$$

The dSPM denominator is the noise standard deviation of source $k$, since the whitened noise has identity covariance [@dale_dynamic_2000]. The sLORETA denominator is the square root of the $k$-th diagonal entry of the resolution matrix [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002]. MNE-Python's sLORETA factor differs from this one by the constant $1/\sqrt\lambda$, which rescales the maps without changing their shape [@gramfort_meg_2013].

**GBF — full formulation.** wCSET (Eq. 4) is reconfigured to approximate GBF via three changes to its own formulation: (i) $\mathbf U$ becomes the Laplace-Beltrami eigenbasis of the cortical mesh (Section 2.1.3) rather than the connectome's; (ii) no depth weighting ($\mathbf W_d = \mathbf I$); and (iii) the exponential weights (Eq. 3) become GBF's hard-truncated, log-form weighting, $W_{h,ii} = \sqrt{-\log(\mu_i/\mu_S)}$ for the $S$ lowest-frequency Beltrami eigenmodes and $W_{h,ii}=0$ beyond ($\mu_i$: Laplace-Beltrami eigenvalues).

**GBF cutoff tuning.** Wang et al. tune a scale parameter $\beta$ for their log-form weighting, but our pipeline trace-renormalizes the inverse kernel before the ridge solve (standard practice), which renders $\beta$ a pure rescale with no effect on the reconstruction. Rather than leave this comparator's one nominally free parameter untuned, we instead tuned the parameter that actually shapes the weighting under our normalization, the cutoff $S$: a sweep against simulated ground truth showed $S=150$ roughly halving peak-localization error relative to $S=300$ (6.1 vs. 14.7 mm) while matching or exceeding it on average precision.

## Datasets and Study-Specific Settings

### Synthetic Data — Data Acquisition and Preprocessing

This section lists the data needed to reproduce the synthetic data described in Section 2.2.1, and the processing applied to it before simulation. The corresponding code is in `processing_simf.qmd` of the manuscript repository ([github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET](https://github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET)).

**Data source.** All subject data come from the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022], publicly available on OpenNeuro as dataset ds003505 ([openneuro.org/datasets/ds003505](https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds003505); paths below as of snapshot 1.1.2). Only one participant, `sub-10`, is used. None of VEPCON's EEG recordings, raw diffusion images or other participants are needed.

| File (relative to the dataset root) | Content | Used for |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `sub-10/anat/sub-10_T1w.nii.gz` | Raw T1-weighted MRI | CHARM tissue segmentation (BEM) |
| `derivatives/freesurfer-7.1.1/sub-10/` | FreeSurfer reconstruction (whole subject folder) | Source space, parcellation, electrode coregistration |
| `derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/dwi/sub-10_model-CSD_desc-DET_tractogram.trk` | Whole-brain tractogram, in diffusion space | Long-range connectome edges |
| `derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/xfm/final0GenericAffine.mat` | Affine registration between T1w and diffusion space (ANTs) | Mapping streamline endpoints to T1w space |

: VEPCON files required for the synthetic data. {#tbl-vepcon-files}

**Tractogram provenance.** The tractogram is used as distributed, without re-running tractography. According to its Connectome Mapper 3 configuration file (`derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/sub-10_diffusion_config.json`), the diffusion data were corrected for eddy currents and motion (FSL `eddy_correct`), without denoising or bias-field correction. Fiber orientations were reconstructed with constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD, maximal harmonic order 4) in MRtrix3. One million streamlines were then generated with deterministic tractography (`SD_stream`; step 0.5 mm, length 5–200 mm, maximum angle 45°, FOD cutoff 0.05), without anatomically-constrained tractography (ACT), and filtered with SIFT. These settings come from a later Connectome Mapper release than the one described in @pascucci_source_2022, and differ from the tractograms that @ruequeralt_connectome_2024 recomputed from the same raw DWI for CSET (10 million streamlines with ACT, after denoising and bias-field correction).

**External resources.** Besides VEPCON, the pipeline uses:

- the EGI 256-channel HydroCel template montage built into MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013], used as sensor layout (no subject-specific electrode positions);
- the Lausanne 2018 scale-4 cortical atlas and the HCP probabilistic thalamic-nuclei atlas, with the MNI ICBM152 2009c template, needed to build the MultiConn parcellation [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022];
- the MultiConn probabilistic connectivity atlas at scale 4 [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], needed only for the atlas surrogate (Section 2.1.3).

**Processing steps.** Everything else is derived from the files above:

1. *Head model.* The T1w is segmented with SimNIBS CHARM [@puonti_accurate_2020], and the three BEM surfaces (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) are built from this segmentation (Volume Conduction Model, below).
2. *Parcellation.* The MultiConn scale-4 parcellation is computed on the FreeSurfer reconstruction (white-matter margin 2 mm; thalamic atlas thresholded at probability 0.05). Its cortical labels provide the cortex mask and the 446 regions used for the probe set.
3. *Source space.* Dipoles are placed on the FreeSurfer white-matter surface (oct6 spacing) and restricted to the cortex mask (Source Space, below).
4. *Electrodes.* The EGI template is reduced by removing the same cheek electrodes as in Clinical Dataset A (Section 2.2.2). It is aligned to the subject with a rigid fiducial-based registration, and each electrode is then projected radially onto the CHARM scalp surface.
5. *Connectome.* Streamline endpoints are mapped from diffusion space to T1w space with the affine transform above (the nonlinear `final1Warp.nii.gz` is not used). Streamlines are kept only if both endpoints fall in the cortex mask. Each remaining endpoint is assigned to a dipole within 4 mm, and each edge is weighted by fiber length. Short-range gray-matter edges are then added where tractography found none (Connectivity Matrices, below).

### Synthetic Data — Additional Simulation Details

This section provides implementation-level detail for the synthetic data described in Section 2.2.1.

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Unit | Description | Ref. |
|:---|:---:|---:|:---:|:---|:---:|
| Spike duration | $W$ | 0.05 | s | Total duration of the double-Hanning-window spike waveform. | [@kane_revised_2017] |
| Axonal conduction speed (long-range) | $v(l>35)$ | 4.5 | mm/ms | Conduction speed for long-range (non-U-fiber) tracts, i.e. edges longer than the U-fiber length cutoff. | [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] |
| U-fiber conduction speed | $v(l\leq35)$ | 2.5 | mm/ms | Conduction speed for short-range U-fibers (edges at or below the U-fiber length cutoff), distinctly slower than long-range tracts. | [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023] |
| U-fiber maximum length | — | 35 | mm | Length cutoff separating U-fibers from long-range tracts. | — |
| Nodal delay per hop | $\tau_p$ | 7 | ms | Per-hop relay delay representing the time a cortical population takes to receive, integrate, and re-fire an input; accumulated once per edge on the propagation path. | [@lemarechal_brain_2022] |
| Spatial decay factor | $\gamma$ | 0.5 | — | Per-hop amplitude decay factor applied to propagating activity; a tuned/free parameter, since no literature value exists for this quantity. | — |
| Delay jitter (s.d., per hop) | $\sigma_\tau$ | 1 | ms | Per-hop timing-jitter standard deviation, accumulated as jitter$\times\sqrt{\text{hops}}$ along the propagation path to avoid deterministic, sample-locked arrival times. | — |
| Sensor noise floor (fixed) | — | 2.0 | µV RMS | Fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor added at the sensor level, independent of the source-space noise contribution. | — |
| Target sensor noise (total) | — | 15.0 | µV RMS | Target total delivered sensor-level background noise (instrument floor plus forward-projected source-space noise). | [@nunez_electric_2006] |
| Target SNR | — | 5 | — | Target single-trial peak-amplitude SNR used to scale source activity before sensor projection. | [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024] |
| Source regions (probe set) | — | 100 | — | Number of source regions simulated, drawn from the shared spatially-uniform (farthest-point-sampled) probe set. | — |
| Repetitions per region | — | 8 | — | Number of repeated simulations per source region (independent noise draws), set via power analysis. | — |

: Simulation parameters. Dashes mark free/tuned parameters with no literature-derived value. {#tbl-sim-params}

**Propagation model rationale.** A neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995] would capture propagation more physiologically, but such models become unstable at high mass counts, since network size and coupling strength jointly determine dynamical stability [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015] — which is why other source-reconstruction studies typically cap the number of masses around 1,000, with dipoles spaced roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026], a spacing at which the forward model's own point-dipole assumption starts to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019]. Our patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model avoids this trade-off, keeping the dipole model at high resolution (~7,600 dipoles, ~3.3 mm spacing) while remaining simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes; we do not claim it is more faithful to reality than neural mass or field models, only that it offers insight a simple patch simulation cannot while staying tractable at high dipole counts.

**Spike waveform.** The spike waveform is a double Hanning window, following the same construction as @dewouters_source-reconstructed_2026:

$$
s_0(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$, and $W = 0.05$ s (50 ms) is the total spike duration, chosen to fall centrally within the consensus clinical EEG duration convention for interictal spikes specifically (20–70 ms) [@kane_revised_2017].

**Propagation delay model.** The total propagation delay $\tau_j$ to dipole $j$ was computed as the sum of per-edge delays along the shortest path from the source:

$$
\tau_j = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_j} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v(l_{uv})} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_\tau, \qquad v(l) = \begin{cases} 4.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l > 35 \text{ mm (long-range)} \\ 2.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l \leq 35 \text{ mm (U-fiber)} \end{cases}
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ in mm, and $v(l_{uv})$ is a conduction speed that depends on fiber length: 4.5 mm/ms for long-range tracts above 35 mm — the central estimate of two independent large-sample cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) studies converging on ~3–6 m/s for adult long-range association fibers [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] — and a slower 2.5 mm/ms for short-range U-fibers at or below 35 mm, reflecting their distinctly slower reported conduction (~2–3 m/s) relative to long-range tracts [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023]. $\tau_p = 7$ ms is a fixed nodal delay per hop representing synaptic transmission plus relay latency, consistent with the population-level excitatory/inhibitory synaptic time constants (5.8–7.3 ms) estimated directly from CCEP modelling [@lemarechal_brain_2022]. $\epsilon_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$, with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms, is a per-dipole jitter term modelling uncertainty in propagation timing, accumulated once per hop along the shortest path (i.e. scaling with $\sqrt{h_j}$ rather than a single flat perturbation of the total path delay).

**Noise model derivation.** Sensor-level noise comprised a small fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor (2.0 µV RMS) plus a source-space contribution solved to bring the total delivered sensor-level baseline noise to a target of 15.0 µV RMS — the literature midpoint of the commonly-cited ~10–20 µV RMS scalp EEG background noise range [@nunez_electric_2006]. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calibrated to a fixed single-trial target of 5 (peak amplitude relative to baseline standard deviation) by scaling the source activity prior to sensor projection: this sits above the ~2.0–3.2 linear-ratio range reported for single-trial interictal spikes [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024], chosen as a practical compromise to keep delivered spikes comfortably above the simulator's own noise floor while remaining much closer to the single-trial literature range than a post-averaging-scale target would be.

**Power analysis.** The number of regions (100) and repetitions (8) per region were set via a power analysis targeting adequate power for the region-paired method comparisons reported throughout the Results, ensuring that the relative ranking of reconstruction methods is robust across a spatially-diverse sample of source regions rather than reflecting any single one; the main effect of method alone was already saturated at power ≈ 1.0 across every tested design.

### Clinical Dataset A — Additional Details

This section provides additional preprocessing detail for the resection cohort described in Section 2.2.2.

**Preprocessing by the data providers.** Data-provider preprocessing (per @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025) included bandpass filtering (high-pass: 0.3–1 Hz; low-pass: 30–100 Hz, with filter settings varying across patients due to the longitudinal nature of the dataset), downsampling to 250 Hz, and interpolation of noisy channels from neighbouring electrodes using 3D splines.

### Clinical Dataset B — Additional Details

This section provides additional recruitment, implantation, and ethics detail for the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort described in Section 2.2.3, drawn from @roehri_scalp-negative_2025, the source study for this cohort.

**Recruitment and implantation.** Patients were recruited at the EEG and Epilepsy Unit, Geneva University Hospital, among consecutive patients who underwent simultaneous iEEG–hdEEG recording between 2014 and 2019 during presurgical evaluation for pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy. Intracranial recordings used stereo-EEG (SEEG) intracerebral macroelectrodes implanted per standard clinical presurgical planning; the simultaneous recording session was performed on the last day before iEEG electrode removal, pairing the SEEG with a 257-channel geodesic scalp EEG net (Electrical Geodesic Inc.).

**Ethics approval.** The study was approved by the Geneva Regional Research Ethics Committee (protocol 13-004).

**MRI sequencing parameters.** The T1-weighted scan was acquired on a 3-T scanner (Siemens Prisma); @roehri_scalp-negative_2025 does not report further sequence parameters (TR/TE/voxel size).

**Comparison window.** The window over which virtual and recorded iEEG were compared was the continuous interval over which the evoked response's global field power (GFP) stayed above 3 standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline.

## Statistical Analysis — Additional Details

**Autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size.** For the paired t-test with effective sample size (used for Study 3's channel/timepoint comparisons), the effective sample size is computed as $n_{\text{eff}} = n / (1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{K} \rho_k)$, where $\rho_k$ is the paired-difference series' own lag-$k$ autocorrelation, summed until it falls within the white-noise 95% confidence band ($1.96/\sqrt{n}$), capped at $n/4$ — the standard correction for testing the mean of a serially-correlated series. This down-weights the nominal pair count to reflect the true amount of independent evidence when neighbouring channels or timepoints are correlated.

**Cluster-based permutation testing.** Continuous comparisons (e.g. across SNR or connectome perturbation severity) used a one-sample, sign-flip permutation test on the paired-difference series (MNE-Python's `permutation_cluster_1samp_test`; 3000 permutations), which identifies contiguous clusters of the coordinate where the two methods differ, rather than testing each point independently. The cluster-forming threshold matched the test's own two-tailed α = 0.05 default; each cluster's p-value reflects how extreme its summed test statistic is relative to the permutation null, and effect size (Cohen's dz) is computed from each subject's difference averaged across the cluster's span.

### Robustness to Data Noise — Full Results (Section 3.1.2)

```{python filename="simf_noise_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

noise_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/noise_sweep")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]
standard = ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]

# Same tests as the main text (index.qmd, simf_noise_summary_stats.py), reloaded from its cache: cluster
# permutation over SNR, wCSET vs. each competitor, region-paired (each region = the mean over its runs), Holm
# across the 4 pairs (family="pair"). sign = +1 = wCSET better.
def _snr_order(metric):
    return sorted(noise_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["snr"].unique(), reverse=True)

def _noise_test(metric, phase, higher_is_better):
    return cached(
        noise_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation, f"../results/simf/noise_sweep/stats/{metric}_{phase}_cluster",
        metric, coord="snr", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=noise_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
        coord_order=_snr_order(metric), higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": phase},
        correction="holm", family="pair", n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

noise_loc_results = _noise_test("localization_error", "qrp", higher_is_better=False)

# Medians as in the main text: one value per region (the mean over its runs), then the median across regions.
def _noise_medians(metric, phase):
    df = noise_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": phase})
    return df.groupby(["Method", "snr", "region"])["Value"].mean().groupby(["Method", "snr"]).median()

_loc_medians = _noise_medians("localization_error", "qrp")
noise_corr_results = {phase: _noise_test("correlation", phase, higher_is_better=True) for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]}

def _cluster(result, competitor, sign):
    """Largest cluster of the given sign (+1 = wCSET better) against `competitor`, or None."""
    clusters = result.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", competitor)]
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == sign] if not clusters.empty else clusters
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

CI_LEVEL = 0.99  # as in the main text: CIs Bonferroni-corrected for families of up to five comparisons

def _cluster_diff(metric, phase, competitor, cluster, higher_is_better):
    """Paired difference over a cluster's SNR span, positive = wCSET better, with its 99% CI: the Hodges-Lehmann
    estimate for localization error and the mean for correlation, as in the main text."""
    snrs = [v for v in _snr_order(metric) if cluster["snr_end"] <= v <= cluster["snr_start"]]
    estimator = noise_metrics.estimate.hodges_lehmann if metric == "localization_error" else noise_metrics.estimate.mean_diff
    return estimator(
        metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=[("wcset", competitor)], pairing_col="region",
        filters={"phase": phase, "snr": snrs}, alpha=1 - CI_LEVEL,
    ).vs("wcset", higher_is_better=higher_is_better).loc[competitor]

def _p(p_corrected):
    """"≤" at the smallest p that 3000 permutations (Holm-corrected) can return, as in the main text."""
    return f"≤ {p_corrected:.3f}" if p_corrected < 0.002 else fmt_p(p_corrected)

_df_loc = noise_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})
noise_n_regions = _df_loc["region"].nunique()
noise_n_runs = int(_df_loc[_df_loc["Method"] == "wcset"].groupby(["snr", "region"]).size().unique().item())
noise_snr_levels = ", ".join(f"{v:g}" for v in _snr_order("localization_error"))

# Localization error. The prose: wMNE worse than wCSET over the whole range; sLORETA and dSPM worse at high SNR
# only; dSPM better at one low SNR without significance; no cluster at all against CSET.
_loc_better = {c: _cluster(noise_loc_results, c, 1) for c in competitors}
_loc_worse = {c: _cluster(noise_loc_results, c, -1) for c in competitors}
assert _loc_better["cset"] is None and _loc_worse["cset"] is None
assert all(_loc_better[c]["significant"] for c in ["wmne", "sloreta", "dspm"])
assert (_loc_better["wmne"]["snr_start"], _loc_better["wmne"]["snr_end"]) == (20, 1)
assert all(w is None or not w["significant"] for w in _loc_worse.values()) and _loc_worse["dspm"] is not None
# "25.0 mm (99% CI 21.2 to 28.7; p_corrected ≤ 0.001)", and each cluster's SNR span
noise_loc = {
    c: f'{fmt_ci(_cluster_diff("localization_error", "qrp", c, _loc_better[c], False), "estimate", unit=" mm", level=CI_LEVEL)[:-1]}'
       f'; p_corrected {_p(_loc_better[c]["p_corrected"])})'
    for c in ["wmne", "sloreta", "dspm"]
}
noise_loc_wmne, noise_loc_sloreta, noise_loc_dspm = (noise_loc[c] for c in ["wmne", "sloreta", "dspm"])
noise_loc_sloreta_end, noise_loc_dspm_end = (fmt_num(_loc_better[c]["snr_end"], 0) for c in ["sloreta", "dspm"])
assert all(_loc_better[c]["snr_start"] == 20 for c in ["sloreta", "dspm"])
noise_loc_dspm_worse_snr = fmt_num(_loc_worse["dspm"]["snr_start"], 0)
noise_loc_dspm_worse_p = fmt_p(_loc_worse["dspm"]["p_corrected"])
_cset_by_snr = [
    noise_metrics.estimate.hodges_lehmann(
        "localization_error", group_by="Method", comparisons=[("wcset", "cset")], pairing_col="region",
        filters={"phase": "qrp", "snr": [v]},
    ).vs("wcset", higher_is_better=False).loc["cset"]
    for v in _snr_order("localization_error")
]
assert all(r["ci_low"] <= 0 <= r["ci_high"] for r in _cset_by_snr)
noise_loc_cset_lo = f'{min(r["estimate"] for r in _cset_by_snr):.1f}'
noise_loc_cset_hi = f'{max(r["estimate"] for r in _cset_by_snr):+.1f}'

# Median localization error (mm) per method and SNR
_four = ["wcset", "cset", "sloreta", "dspm"]
noise_loc_four_20_lo, noise_loc_four_20_hi = (fmt_num(f(_loc_medians[m, 20] for m in _four)) for f in [min, max])
noise_loc_four_1_lo, noise_loc_four_1_hi = (fmt_num(f(_loc_medians[m, 1] for m in _four)) for f in [min, max])
noise_loc_wmne_median20, noise_loc_wmne_median5, noise_loc_wmne_median1 = (fmt_num(_loc_medians["wmne", v]) for v in [20, 5, 1])
noise_loc_wcset_median10, noise_loc_wcset_median5 = (fmt_num(_loc_medians["wcset", v]) for v in [10, 5])
noise_loc_wcset_median3, noise_loc_dspm_median3 = (fmt_num(_loc_medians[m, 3]) for m in ["wcset", "dspm"])
noise_loc_dspm_median_lo, noise_loc_dspm_median_hi = (fmt_num(f(_loc_medians["dspm"].loc[5:])) for f in [min, max])

# Spatial correlation, both phases. The prose: wCSET better than every competitor down to some SNR, then
# slightly worse (all significant); the minimum-norm methods level off above wCSET and CSET at the lowest SNRs.
_corr_medians_qrp, _corr_medians_pp = (_noise_medians("correlation", ph) for ph in ["qrp", "pp"])
_corr_medians = {"qrp": _corr_medians_qrp, "pp": _corr_medians_pp}
noise_corr_wcset_qrp20, noise_corr_wcset_qrp1 = (fmt_num(_corr_medians_qrp["wcset", v], 2) for v in [20, 1])
noise_corr_wcset_pp20, noise_corr_wcset_pp1 = (fmt_num(_corr_medians_pp["wcset", v], 2) for v in [20, 1])
noise_corr_cset_pp20 = fmt_num(_corr_medians_pp["cset", 20], 2)
noise_corr_std_lo, noise_corr_std_hi = (
    fmt_num(f(_corr_medians[ph][m].loc[v] for ph in _corr_medians for m in standard for v in _snr_order("correlation")), 2)
    for f in [min, max])
noise_corr_std_1_lo, noise_corr_std_1_hi = (fmt_num(f(_corr_medians[ph][m, 1] for ph in _corr_medians for m in standard), 2) for f in [min, max])
noise_corr_cw_1_hi = fmt_num(max(_corr_medians[ph][m, 1] for ph in _corr_medians for m in ["wcset", "cset"]), 2)

_corr_better = {(ph, c): _cluster(noise_corr_results[ph], c, 1) for ph in noise_corr_results for c in competitors}
_corr_worse = {(ph, c): _cluster(noise_corr_results[ph], c, -1) for ph in noise_corr_results for c in competitors}
assert all(b is not None and b["significant"] and b["snr_start"] == 20 for b in _corr_better.values())
assert all(w is not None and w["significant"] and w["snr_start"] < _corr_better[k]["snr_end"] for k, w in _corr_worse.items())
noise_corr_end_std = fmt_num(max(_corr_better[(ph, c)]["snr_end"] for ph in noise_corr_results for c in standard), 0)
noise_corr_end_cset = fmt_num(max(_corr_better[(ph, "cset")]["snr_end"] for ph in noise_corr_results), 0)
noise_corr_p_max = _p(max(b["p_corrected"] for b in _corr_better.values()))
_corr_d = {k: _cluster_diff("correlation", k[0], k[1], b, True)["estimate"] for k, b in _corr_better.items()}
noise_corr_std_d_lo, noise_corr_std_d_hi = (fmt_num(f(d for (_, c), d in _corr_d.items() if c in standard), 2) for f in [min, max])
noise_corr_cset_d_qrp, noise_corr_cset_d_pp = (fmt_num(_corr_d[(ph, "cset")], 2) for ph in ["qrp", "pp"])
_worse_d = {k: -_cluster_diff("correlation", k[0], k[1], w, True)["estimate"] for k, w in _corr_worse.items()}
noise_corr_worse_std_lo, noise_corr_worse_std_hi = (fmt_num(f(d for (_, c), d in _worse_d.items() if c in standard), 2) for f in [min, max])
assert all(d < 0.01 for (_, c), d in _worse_d.items() if c == "cset")
noise_corr_worse_p_max = f'{max(w["p_corrected"] for w in _corr_worse.values()):.3f}'
```

We repeated the Study I simulation for `{python} noise_n_regions` of its 100 regions at single-spike SNRs of `{python} noise_snr_levels`, with `{python} noise_n_runs` runs per region at each SNR (Section 2.2.1). The tests are those of the main text: each region is summarized by the mean over its runs, and a cluster-based permutation test over SNR compares wCSET with each competitor, region-paired and Holm-corrected across the four competitors. Over each cluster's SNR span, differences in localization error are Hodges–Lehmann shifts and differences in spatial correlation are mean paired differences, both positive when wCSET is better. The figures show the median across regions.

At SNR 20, wCSET, CSET, sLORETA and dSPM all localized well, with median errors of `{python} noise_loc_four_20_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_four_20_hi` mm (@fig-annex-noise-loc). wMNE started at `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median20` mm but degraded first: its median rose to `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median5` mm at SNR 5 and `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median1` mm at SNR 1, and wCSET localized more accurately than wMNE at every SNR, by `{python} noise_loc_wmne`. The other four methods degraded later and reached `{python} noise_loc_four_1_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_four_1_hi` mm at SNR 1. At high SNR, wCSET localized more accurately than sLORETA from SNR 20 to `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_sloreta`, and than dSPM from SNR 20 to `{python} noise_loc_dspm_end`, by `{python} noise_loc_dspm`. Its median error rose from `{python} noise_loc_wcset_median10` mm at SNR 10 to `{python} noise_loc_wcset_median5` mm at SNR 5, whereas dSPM's stayed at `{python} noise_loc_dspm_median_lo`–`{python} noise_loc_dspm_median_hi` mm from SNR 20 down to 5. At SNR `{python} noise_loc_dspm_worse_snr`, dSPM's median error (`{python} noise_loc_dspm_median3` mm) was below wCSET's (`{python} noise_loc_wcset_median3` mm), but this reversal was not significant (p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_dspm_worse_p`). wCSET and CSET did not differ at any SNR: no cluster formed, and the per-SNR differences ranged from `{python} noise_loc_cset_lo` to `{python} noise_loc_cset_hi` mm (positive = wCSET better), with every 95% CI including zero.

Spatial correlation separated the methods more clearly (@fig-annex-noise-corr). wCSET's median correlation fell from `{python} noise_corr_wcset_qrp20` at the quarter rising phase and `{python} noise_corr_wcset_pp20` at the peak at SNR 20 to `{python} noise_corr_wcset_qrp1` at SNR 1. CSET followed the same course at lower values (`{python} noise_corr_cset_pp20` at the peak at SNR 20), whereas the minimum-norm methods stayed between `{python} noise_corr_std_lo` and `{python} noise_corr_std_hi` across the whole range. From SNR 20, wCSET's correlation was higher than the minimum-norm methods' down to SNR `{python} noise_corr_end_std` and than CSET's down to SNR `{python} noise_corr_end_cset`, at both phases (all p_corrected `{python} noise_corr_p_max`). Over these clusters, it exceeded the minimum-norm methods' by Δr = `{python} noise_corr_std_d_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_std_d_hi` and CSET's by Δr = `{python} noise_corr_cset_d_qrp` at the quarter rising phase and `{python} noise_corr_cset_d_pp` at the peak. At the lowest SNRs, the spike could no longer be distinguished from the noise. wCSET's and CSET's correlations fell to at most `{python} noise_corr_cw_1_hi`, whereas the minimum-norm methods' leveled off at `{python} noise_corr_std_1_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_std_1_hi`, so wCSET's was slightly lower than theirs (Δr = `{python} noise_corr_worse_std_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_worse_std_hi`) and differed from CSET's by less than 0.01 (all p_corrected ≤ `{python} noise_corr_worse_p_max`).

### Robustness to Prior Noise — Full Results (Section 3.1.3)

```{python filename="simf_degradation_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm
import numpy as np

deg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/degradation")

# Same tests as the main text (index.qmd, simf_degradation_summary_stats.py), reloaded from its cache: cluster
# permutation over perturbation level, CSET/wCSET vs. each connectome-agnostic reference (sLORETA, dSPM),
# region-paired (each region = the mean over its runs), Holm across the 4 pairs (family="pair"). Localization
# error at the quarter rising phase, spatial correlation at the peak. The reference comes first in each pair, so
# sign = -1 means CSET/wCSET is better.
DEG_PHASE = {"localization_error": "qrp", "correlation": "pp"}
DEG_REFERENCES = ["sloreta", "dspm"]

def _deg_test(metric, higher_is_better):
    phase = DEG_PHASE[metric]
    order = sorted(deg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": phase})["percentage"].unique())
    return cached(
        deg_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation, f"../results/simf/degradation/stats/{metric}_{phase}_cluster",
        metric, coord="percentage", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=deg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(DEG_REFERENCES, ["cset", "wcset"]),
        pairing_col="region", coord_order=order, higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": phase},
        correction="holm", family="pair", n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

deg_results = {"localization_error": _deg_test("localization_error", False), "correlation": _deg_test("correlation", True)}
deg_n_regions = deg_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error")["region"].nunique()
```

```{python filename="simf_degradation_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DEG_METHODS = ["wcset", "cset", "sloreta", "dspm"]
DEG_PAIRS = [("sloreta", "wcset"), ("dspm", "wcset"), ("sloreta", "cset"), ("dspm", "cset")]

def degradation_figure(metric, ylabel):
    """Median across regions (each region = the mean over its runs) with an IQR band per method, and below it one
    row of significant clusters per pair (colored: CSET/wCSET better than the reference, gray: worse)."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    deg_metrics.plot.line(
        metric, "percentage", hue="Method", unit="region", hue_order=DEG_METHODS, center="median", interval="iqr",
        highlight="wcset", palette=COLORS, fill_alpha=0.15, labels=METHOD_LABELS, filters={"phase": DEG_PHASE[metric]},
        ax=ax,
    )
    ax.legend(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.6), fontsize=8, frameon=False)
    result = deg_results[metric]
    levels = np.asarray(result.coord_order, dtype=float)
    step = (levels[1] - levels[0]) / 2
    dy = np.ptp(ax.get_ylim())
    row_h, row0 = 0.035 * dy, ax.get_ylim()[0] - 0.04 * dy
    for k, (ref, method) in enumerate(DEG_PAIRS):
        y = row0 - (k + 1) * 1.4 * row_h
        cl = result.clusters_by_pair[(ref, method)]
        for _, row in cl[cl["significant"].astype(bool)].iterrows():
            better = row["sign"] < 0
            ax.fill_between([row["percentage_start"] - step, row["percentage_end"] + step], y, y + row_h,
                            color=matte(COLORS[method]) if better else "#c3c2b7", linewidth=0, zorder=2)
        ax.text(levels[0] - 2 * step, y + row_h / 2, f"{METHOD_LABELS[method]} vs. {METHOD_LABELS[ref]}", fontsize=7,
                ha="right", va="center", color="#444444")
    yticks = [v for v in ax.get_yticks() if row0 <= v <= ax.get_ylim()[1]]
    ax.set_ylim(row0 - (len(DEG_PAIRS) + 0.6) * 1.4 * row_h, ax.get_ylim()[1])
    ax.set_yticks(yticks)
    ax.set_xticks(levels)
    ax.set_xlabel("Connectome edges swapped (%)")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig
```

### Surrogate alternatives — Full Results (Section 3.1.4)

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_full_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# self-contained, like the other "Full Results" Annex sections above -
# reloads and recomputes independently of the main-text surrogate cell
# rather than reusing its variables (same identical calls, disk-cache hit).
surrogates_full = ["beltrami", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
conditions_full = ["original"] + surrogates_full

# same reader-facing renaming as the main-text cell (Section 3.1.4) - fused/
# fused-bin/geom-atlas/geom-atlas-bin are the on-disk `Surrogate` tags.
SURROGATE_LABELS_FULL = {
    "beltrami": "Beltrami (GBF)", "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}

surr_metrics_full = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/surrogates")
surr_comparisons_full = surr_metrics_full.stat.build_comparisons(["original"], surrogates_full)

# CSET's own breakdown - wCSET's is reported in full in the main text.
surr_loc_cset = surr_metrics_full.stat.wilcoxon(
    "localization_error", group_by="Surrogate",
    comparisons=surr_comparisons_full, pairing_col="region",
    filters={"Method": "cset", "phase": "qrp"},
)
surr_corr_cset = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    surr_corr_cset[phase] = surr_metrics_full.stat.wilcoxon(
        "correlation", group_by="Surrogate",
        comparisons=surr_comparisons_full, pairing_col="region",
        filters={"Method": "cset", "phase": phase},
    )

# statistics quoted in the prose below (effects as stored: original - surrogate).
_loc_cset = surr_loc_cset.vs("original")
_corr_cset = {ph: surr_corr_cset[ph].vs("original") for ph in ["qrp", "pp"]}
loc_cset_p = {s: fmt_p(_loc_cset.loc[s, "p_corrected"]) for s in surrogates_full}
loc_cset_r = {s: fmt_stat(_loc_cset.loc[s, "effect"]) for s in surrogates_full}
corr_cset_p = {(s, ph): fmt_p(_corr_cset[ph].loc[s, "p_corrected"]) for ph in _corr_cset for s in surrogates_full}
corr_cset_r = {(s, ph): fmt_stat(_corr_cset[ph].loc[s, "effect"]) for ph in _corr_cset for s in surrogates_full}

# wCSET's spatial correlation at the quarter rising phase (the main text shows the peak only).
surr_corr_wcset_qrp = surr_metrics_full.stat.wilcoxon(
    "correlation", group_by="Surrogate",
    comparisons=surr_comparisons_full, pairing_col="region",
    filters={"Method": "wcset", "phase": "qrp"},
)

# dSPM's and sLORETA's benchmark reference lines, summarized like the boxes (as in the main text):
# one value per run, mean over repetitions per region, median across regions. Correlation: each run's
# curve read at the population median qrp/peak time.
# Correlation: per-region curves (mean over repetitions) read at the population median qrp/peak time,
# which fall on the 4 ms time grid.
import numpy as np
_flag_full = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/flagship")
_ref_methods_full = ["dspm", "sloreta"]
surr_ref_loc_full = (_flag_full.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp", "Method": _ref_methods_full})
                     .groupby(["Method", "region"])["Value"].mean().groupby("Method").median().to_dict())
_curves_full = (_flag_full.to_df(metrics="correlation", filters={"Method": _ref_methods_full})
                .groupby(["Method", "region", "times"], as_index=False)["Value"].mean())
_grid_full = np.sort(_curves_full["times"].unique())
surr_ref_corr_full = {}
for _phase, _key in [("qrp", "qrp_time_median"), ("pp", "pp_time_median")]:
    _t = _flag_full.metadata["derived"][_key]
    _tg = _grid_full[np.argmin(np.abs(_grid_full - _t))]
    assert abs(_tg - _t) < 1e-4  # on the grid, so no interpolation is needed
    surr_ref_corr_full[_phase] = _curves_full[_curves_full["times"] == _tg].groupby("Method")["Value"].median().to_dict()
```

This section reports CSET's full surrogate-connectome breakdown (@fig-annex-surrogate-cset), summarized qualitatively in the main text alongside wCSET's own (Section 3.1.4), which is reported there in full.

For localization error, CSET was significantly less accurate with the Laplace-Beltrami surrogate (GBF; p_corrected `{python} loc_cset_p['beltrami']`, r = `{python} loc_cset_r['beltrami']`) and the local surrogate (p_corrected `{python} loc_cset_p['geom-atlas']`, r = `{python} loc_cset_r['geom-atlas']`); the atlas, atlas-bin, and local-bin surrogates did not differ significantly from the original connectome (p_corrected `{python} loc_cset_p['fused']`, `{python} loc_cset_p['fused-bin']`, and `{python} loc_cset_p['geom-atlas-bin']` respectively).

For spatial correlation, CSET was significantly lower than the original connectome with the atlas surrogate at both the quarter rising phase (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused', 'qrp')]`) and the peak (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused', 'pp')]`), and likewise with the local (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas', 'qrp')]` and `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas', 'pp')]`) and local-bin (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas-bin', 'qrp')]` and `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas-bin', 'pp')]`) surrogates at both phases. The atlas-bin surrogate reached significance only at the peak (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused-bin', 'pp')]`), not at the quarter rising phase (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused-bin', 'qrp')]`). The Laplace-Beltrami surrogate never differed significantly from the original connectome, at either phase (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('beltrami', 'qrp')]` and `{python} corr_cset_p[('beltrami', 'pp')]`).

### Prior Similarity of Surrogate and Perturbed Connectomes (Sections 3.1.3–3.1.4)

```{python filename="simf_prior_similarity_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Similarities computed by processing_simf.qmd ("Prior Similarity"): the individual prior against each perturbed
# connectome and each surrogate, with every harmonic ("similarity") and without the λ = 0 harmonics
# ("similarity_nonzero"), plus each connectome's smallest nonzero eigenvalue and the share of its prior held by the
# λ = 0 harmonics.
prior_sim = pd.read_csv("../results/simf/prior_similarity/similarity.csv")
_pert = prior_sim[prior_sim["kind"] == "perturbation"].set_index("percentage").sort_index()
_surr = prior_sim[prior_sim["kind"] == "surrogate"].set_index("connectome")
PRIOR_SIM_VERSIONS = ["similarity", "similarity_nonzero"]

# Equivalent perturbation: the share of swapped edges at which the perturbation curve reaches the surrogate's
# similarity, by linear interpolation between the tested levels. Both curves decrease monotonically.
for col in PRIOR_SIM_VERSIONS:
    assert (np.diff(_pert[col]) < 0).all()
prior_sim_equiv = pd.DataFrame({
    col: np.interp(-_surr[col], -_pert[col].to_numpy(), _pert.index.to_numpy()) for col in PRIOR_SIM_VERSIONS
}, index=_surr.index)

# The surrogates split into the same two groups in both versions: atlas and the two local surrogates are closest
# to the individual prior, atlas-bin and GBF further away.
prior_sim_close, prior_sim_far = ["fused", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"], ["fused-bin", "beltrami"]
for col in PRIOR_SIM_VERSIONS:
    assert _surr.loc[prior_sim_close, col].min() > _surr.loc[prior_sim_far, col].max()

def _range(values, digits, scale=1):
    lo, hi = fmt_num(min(values) * scale, digits), fmt_num(max(values) * scale, digits)
    return lo if lo == hi else f"{lo}–{hi}"

def _sim(col, pct):
    return fmt_num(_pert.loc[pct, col], 2)

ps_all, ps_nz = "similarity", "similarity_nonzero"
# curves: with every harmonic, the similarity falls fast and levels off; without λ = 0, it falls slowly, then to ~0
ps_all_10, ps_all_30, ps_all_100 = _sim(ps_all, 10), _sim(ps_all, 30), _sim(ps_all, 100)
ps_nz_40, ps_nz_70, ps_nz_100 = _sim(ps_nz, 40), _sim(ps_nz, 70), _sim(ps_nz, 100)
assert (np.diff(_pert.loc[50:, ps_all]) > -0.05).all()  # levels off from 50% on

# mechanism: swaps open a spectral gap, pushing the prior's weight onto the λ = 0 harmonic
ps_lambda_orig = fmt_num(_pert.loc[0, "lambda_min_nonzero"], 3)
ps_lambda_10, ps_lambda_50 = fmt_num(_pert.loc[10, "lambda_min_nonzero"], 2), fmt_num(_pert.loc[50, "lambda_min_nonzero"], 2)
ps_share_orig = fmt_num(_pert.loc[0, "zero_share"] * 100, 0)
ps_share_10, ps_share_30 = fmt_num(_pert.loc[10, "zero_share"] * 100, 0), fmt_num(_pert.loc[30, "zero_share"] * 100, 0)
ps_share_50 = fmt_num(_pert.loc[50, "zero_share"] * 100, 1)
ps_share_graph = _range(_surr.loc[["fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"], "zero_share"], 0, 100)
ps_share_gbf = fmt_num(_surr.loc["beltrami", "zero_share"] * 100, 0)
ps_floor = fmt_num(np.sqrt(_pert.loc[0, "zero_share"]), 2)  # the λ = 0 harmonic's contribution alone: 1 / ‖w₀²‖
assert abs(float(ps_floor) - _pert.loc[100, ps_all]) < 0.01

# surrogates: similarities and equivalent perturbation per version and group
ps_close_all, ps_close_nz = _range(_surr.loc[prior_sim_close, ps_all], 2), _range(_surr.loc[prior_sim_close, ps_nz], 2)
ps_far_all, ps_far_nz = _range(_surr.loc[prior_sim_far, ps_all], 2), _range(_surr.loc[prior_sim_far, ps_nz], 2)
ps_close_all_eq, ps_close_nz_eq = _range(prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_close, ps_all], 0), _range(prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_close, ps_nz], 0)
ps_far_all_eq, ps_far_nz_eq = _range(prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_far, ps_all], 0), _range(prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_far, ps_nz], 0)
ps_eq_min, ps_eq_max = fmt_num(prior_sim_equiv.to_numpy().min(), 0), fmt_num(prior_sim_equiv.to_numpy().max(), 0)

# where those levels fall in the perturbation experiment (the degradation tests reloaded above): wCSET's correlation
# advantage over both references, and its localization advantage over sLORETA
def _better_end(metric, refs):
    ends = []
    for ref in refs:
        cl = deg_results[metric].clusters_by_pair[(ref, "wcset")]
        cl = cl[cl["significant"].astype(bool) & (cl["sign"] < 0)]
        assert len(cl) == 1 and cl["percentage_start"].iloc[0] == 0
        ends.append(cl["percentage_end"].iloc[0])
    return min(ends)

def _worse_start(metric, ref):
    cl = deg_results[metric].clusters_by_pair[(ref, "wcset")]
    cl = cl[cl["significant"].astype(bool) & (cl["sign"] > 0)]
    assert len(cl) == 1
    return cl["percentage_start"].iloc[0]

ps_corr_end = fmt_num(_better_end("correlation", DEG_REFERENCES), 0)
ps_loc_end = fmt_num(_better_end("localization_error", ["sloreta"]), 0)
ps_loc_worse = fmt_num(_worse_start("localization_error", "sloreta"), 0)
assert prior_sim_equiv.to_numpy().max() < float(ps_corr_end)
assert prior_sim_equiv[ps_all].max() <= float(ps_loc_end)
assert prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_close, ps_nz].max() < float(ps_loc_end)
assert float(ps_loc_end) <= prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_far, ps_nz].min() < prior_sim_equiv.loc[prior_sim_far, ps_nz].max() < float(ps_loc_worse)
```

The perturbation experiment (Section 3.1.3) measures connectome errors as a share of swapped edges, which has no equivalent for the surrogates (Section 3.1.4): they differ from the individual connectome in edge count, weights and topology at once. To place them on the same scale, we compared the priors themselves. wCSET uses a connectome only through its prior covariance, Σ = U diag(w²) Uᵀ, with U the connectome's harmonics and w their weights (the low-pass exp(−5λ) for connectome harmonics and GBF's log-decay with a cutoff of 150 for the geometric ones, as in the runs). We measured the similarity of two priors as the cosine similarity of their covariance matrices, sim(Σ₁, Σ₂) = Σᵢⱼ w₁ᵢ² w₂ⱼ² (u₁ᵢ · u₂ⱼ)² / (‖w₁²‖ ‖w₂²‖). It compares every harmonic of one connectome with every harmonic of the other, weighted by how much each prior trusts them, so it needs no harmonic matching and lets each connectome keep its own frequency scale; it equals 1 for identical priors. Depth weighting, the same for every connectome, was left out, and so was CSET, whose unweighted prior makes the measure 1 for any connectome. We compared the individual prior with the prior of each perturbed connectome and of each surrogate, and read each surrogate's equivalent perturbation off the perturbation curve by linear interpolation. Since the λ = 0 harmonic carries the largest weight (w = 1) but only reflects the dipoles' degrees, which edge swaps preserve, we computed the similarity twice: with every harmonic, and without the λ = 0 harmonics.

The two versions describe perturbation differently (@fig-annex-prior-sim). With every harmonic, the similarity fell from 1 to `{python} ps_all_10` at 10% perturbation and `{python} ps_all_30` at 30%, then levelled off at `{python} ps_all_100`. Without the λ = 0 harmonic, it stayed above `{python} ps_nz_40` up to 40% and only fell steeply afterwards, to `{python} ps_nz_70` at 70% and `{python} ps_nz_100` at 100%. The difference comes from the spectrum: random swaps add long-range shortcuts, which raise the smallest nonzero eigenvalue from `{python} ps_lambda_orig` in the individual connectome to `{python} ps_lambda_10` at 10% and `{python} ps_lambda_50` at 50%. The low-pass weights then switch off nearly every harmonic except λ = 0, whose share of the prior grew from `{python} ps_share_orig`% to `{python} ps_share_10`% at 10%, `{python} ps_share_30`% at 30% and `{python} ps_share_50`% at 50%. With every harmonic, the similarity therefore mostly tracks this collapse of the prior onto the λ = 0 harmonic, and its floor (`{python} ps_all_100`) is that harmonic's contribution alone. Without it, the similarity tracks how much the shapes of the remaining harmonics change, which happens later.

The surrogates fell into the same two groups in both versions. The atlas and both local surrogates were closest to the individual prior (similarity `{python} ps_close_all` with every harmonic, `{python} ps_close_nz` without λ = 0), and atlas-bin and GBF were further away (`{python} ps_far_all` and `{python} ps_far_nz`). Their equivalent perturbation, however, depended on the version: `{python} ps_close_all_eq`% for the close group and `{python} ps_far_all_eq`% for atlas-bin and GBF with every harmonic, against `{python} ps_close_nz_eq`% and `{python} ps_far_nz_eq`% without λ = 0. The graph surrogates keep a spectrum close to the individual one (`{python} ps_share_graph`% of the prior in the λ = 0 harmonic, against `{python} ps_share_orig`% for the individual connectome), so they score well when the spectral collapse dominates the measure, and less well when only the shapes of the harmonics count. GBF's λ = 0 harmonics, one constant per hemisphere, hold `{python} ps_share_gbf`% of its prior, which is why it gains the most when they are removed.

The equivalent perturbation is therefore only a rough bracket, between `{python} ps_eq_min`% and `{python} ps_eq_max`% depending on the surrogate and the version. In both versions, every surrogate falls well short of the `{python} ps_corr_end`% up to which wCSET kept its correlation advantage over sLORETA and dSPM in the perturbation experiment, and the close group falls within the range where wCSET was more accurate than sLORETA in localization (up to `{python} ps_loc_end`%). Atlas-bin and GBF fall within that range with every harmonic, but between `{python} ps_loc_end`% and `{python} ps_loc_worse`% without λ = 0, where wCSET was neither significantly better nor worse than sLORETA. The similarity compares priors, not reconstructions, so these equivalents locate the surrogates on the perturbation scale but do not predict their accuracy.

```{python filename="simf_prior_similarity_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-annex-prior-sim
#| fig-cap: "Similarity between wCSET's prior built on the individual connectome and on perturbed or surrogate connectomes (cosine similarity of the prior covariance matrices; 1 = identical priors), (a) with every harmonic and (b) without the λ = 0 harmonics. Black line: perturbed connectomes versus the share of edges swapped. Colored dashed lines: surrogates; each ends at its equivalent perturbation (dot), read off the black line by linear interpolation."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2), sharey=True)
titles = {ps_all: "a. Every harmonic", ps_nz: "b. Without the λ = 0 harmonics"}
for ax, col in zip(axes, PRIOR_SIM_VERSIONS):
    ax.plot(_pert.index, _pert[col], color="#333333", marker="o", markersize=4, label="Perturbed connectome", zorder=3)
    for s in surrogates_full:
        y, x = _surr.loc[s, col], prior_sim_equiv.loc[s, col]
        color = CONDITION_COLORS_FULL[s]
        ax.plot([0, x], [y, y], color=color, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=SURROGATE_LABELS_FULL[s])
        ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=color, markersize=6, zorder=4)
    ax.set_xticks(_pert.index)
    ax.set_xlabel("Connectome edges swapped (%)")
    ax.set_title(titles[col], loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Prior similarity to the individual connectome")
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1.03)
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python filename="intra_window_full_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm
from IPython.display import Markdown

# Same test as the main text (index.qmd, results_intra_vieeg_significance.py), for every patient and competitor: the
# window mean of the signed spatial correlation, wCSET vs. each competitor, paired bootstrap over bursts of spikes
# (processing_intra.qmd, "Spike-level bootstrap"), Holm across the 5 competitors, mean difference with its basic CI
# at CI_LEVEL (99%, as in the main text).
S3_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34", "12", "50"]
S3_PATIENTS = {"48": "1", "34": "2", "12": "3 (deep source)", "50": "4 (deep source)"}
S3_COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]
S3_WINDOW = "correlation_spatial_signed_window"

s3_boot = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/intra/bootstrap")
s3_vs = {
    sub: s3_boot.stat.bootstrap(
        S3_WINDOW, group_by="Method", comparisons=s3_boot.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], S3_COMPETITORS),
        pairing_col="Subject", filters={"Subject": sub}, replicates=f"{S3_WINDOW}_boot", replicate_col="draw",
        estimator="mean_diff", correction="holm", ci_method="basic", ci_level=CI_LEVEL,
    ).vs("wcset")  # positive = wCSET better
    for sub in S3_SUBJECTS
}

def _s3_level(sub, method):
    return s3_boot.to_df(metrics=S3_WINDOW, filters={"Subject": sub, "Method": method})["Value"].item() + 0.0

# @tbl-annex-s3-window: one block per patient, wCSET first, then each competitor with its difference and p_corrected
_rows = []
for sub in S3_SUBJECTS:
    _rows.append([S3_PATIENTS[sub], METHOD_LABELS["wcset"], fmt_num(_s3_level(sub, "wcset"), 2), "", ""])
    for c in S3_COMPETITORS:
        v = s3_vs[sub].loc[c]
        _rows.append(["", METHOD_LABELS[c], fmt_num(round(_s3_level(sub, c), 2) + 0.0, 2),  # + 0.0: no "-0.00"
                      f"{v['mean_diff']:.2f} ({v['mean_diff_ci_low']:.2f} to {v['mean_diff_ci_high']:.2f})",
                      f"{v['p_corrected']:.3f}" + (" *" if v["significant"] else "")])
s3_table = "\n".join(
    [f"| Patient | Method | r (window mean) | wCSET − method ({CI_LEVEL * 100:g}% CI) | p_corrected |",
     "|:--|:--|--:|:--|--:|"] + ["| " + " | ".join(r_) + " |" for r_ in _rows])
s3_n_boot = f'{s3_boot.metadata["bootstrap"]["n_boot"]:,}'
```

This section reports the main text's Study III comparison in full: the signed spatial correlation between virtual and recorded iEEG, averaged over the comparison window, for every patient and method, with every difference from wCSET (@tbl-annex-s3-window). The tests are those of the main text: a paired bootstrap over bursts of spikes (`{python} s3_n_boot` draws), Holm-corrected across the five competitors within each patient, with Bonferroni-corrected 99% basic CIs. The main text quotes the ranges of these values. Patients 3 and 4 had deep sources, far from the cortical source space, so no method's virtual iEEG agreed with their recordings.

